events.text: Above the clouds the Regressor's Guide grows heavy in your hands, and a stranger in grey robes stops you on a bridge of white jade. "That notebook," {npc} says, "is on my shelf. I am a Recorder of the Wheel: I keep the lives that turn again. Yours has pages missing."

effects.log: "The end," {npc} says. "Someone tore it out. I would like to know who." So would you.
You close the notebook and step back. {npc} only bows. "I keep records," {he} says. "I do not take them."

events.text: {npc}, a Recorder of the Wheel, finds you on a bridge of white jade and stares at the notebook in your hands. "I have seen this handwriting finish its last page once before," {he} says slowly. "In another life of yours. You wrote it, and then you came back, and the Guide came back with you."

effects.log: "Something kind," {npc} says. "I will not tell you the rest. You will want to find it yourself." You do.
"Nobody does," {npc} says. "That is what the Guide is for." The notebook feels warm.

events.text: {npc} leads you through an archive where notebooks sit on shelves of cloud. "Every regressor gets a Guide," {he} says. "Most use it to win. A few use it to save people. The torn pages say which you are. Before we look for them: why do you read it?"

effects.log: "Then we look for the pages that warn," {npc} says, and pulls one loose from a shelf of storms.

choices.text: To understand why it came to me

effects.log: "Then we look for the pages that remember," {npc} says, and finds one folded inside an empty Guide.

events.text: A torn page shows a disaster above the clouds that has not happened yet: a floating isle with a village of servants on it, falling. The Guide is never wrong about the ones it shows you true. {npc} reads it over your shoulder. "It falls in three days," {he} says. "Heaven will not stop it. Will you?"

choices.text: Go and hold the isle up

effects.log: You spend three days and most of your energy under the isle like a pillar. It does not fall. The servants never learn your name.

choices.text: Warn them and let it fall

effects.log: Everyone walks off the isle before it goes. You watch it sink into the clouds. The page was right, and nobody was on it.

events.text: A torn page is not a warning at all. It is a letter, in your own older hand: "I read ahead my whole first life and lived none of it. If you are reading this, put the Guide down for a year." {npc} watches you read it twice.

choices.text: Put the Guide down for a year

effects.log: You put it in a drawer and live a year without knowing. It is frightening, and you have rarely been happier.
You keep reading. Behind the letter is another torn page, smaller. {npc} sighs, but does not stop you.

events.text: Every torn page is back in the Guide, and behind the last one is a page that has never been written on. {npc} puts a pen beside it. "This is the last page," {he} says. "Whatever you write here, every page before it becomes true. It is the only page a regressor writes forward."

effects.log: The ink sinks in. The Guide is not a guess any more. {npc} writes the date in a ledger of the Wheel.
You write it, and the Guide seems to breathe out. Its pages will all be true now. You are not sure that is the point any more.

events.text: In the Divine Realm the archive of the Wheel has no walls, only shelves going up forever, and {npc} has climbed with you to the top. The last page of the Guide is blank and shining. "The gods read ahead too," {he} says. "None of them ever wrote the last page. Write it."

choices.text: Write it for every regressor after you

effects.log: You write a single line for the next ones. The shelves hum. {npc} copies it into every Guide below.
You write it small, for yourself. It is enough. The Guide will not lie to you again.

events.text: Years later {npc} visits with tea and a question. "The pages you read warned you," {he} says, "and you changed what was coming. Was it worth knowing?" Below the clouds, people who never met you are alive because of a page.

effects.log: "Good," {npc} says, and writes your answer down. "I will tell the next one that." The Guide closes softly on the table.

choices.text: Say you would rather have not known

effects.log: {npc} nods slowly. "That is what the last one said too," {he} says. "Then they wrote the first page for you."

events.text: {npc} comes to the drawer where you keep the Guide now and finds it closed. "You stopped reading," {he} says. "It is the first time in the archive I have seen a regressor stop." There is one blank page left. The pen is still beside it.

choices.text: Leave the pen where it is

effects.log: You leave it. {npc} smiles for the first time since you met. "Then I will leave the shelf empty a while," {he} says.

mem.note: was given the Guide to keep

effects.log: {npc} takes the notebook in both hands, like something living. "I will keep it on the shelf," {he} says. "Until you want it."

events.text: Above the clouds the loom behind your eyes slows, then stops, as if it has heard a bigger one. Across the valley of clouds there is a loom as wide as a mountain, and at its shuttle sits {npc}. "Ah," {he} calls. "One of my little copies. Come and see where the threads really go."

choices.text: Cross the clouds to the loom

effects.log: Up close the threads are lives, thousands, humming. {npc} makes room on the bench for you.

choices.text: Call back that yours is no copy

effects.log: "Every loom thinks that," {npc} laughs. "Come anyway." You do, eventually.

events.text: {npc}, the Weaver of the Loom of Heaven, looks up from the shuttle as you come over the clouds and goes very still. "I have woven your thread to its end once," {he} says. "In another life. You chose the last glimpse then. And still the loom brought you back."

effects.log: "Everything you did not choose," {npc} says. "You laughed." You find that you believe it.
"They all are," {npc} says, and hands you a spool. "That is what makes them worth weaving."

events.text: {npc} shows you how the great loom works: a glimpse is only a thread pulled forward a little way, to see the colour. "Yours shows you likely paths," {he} says. "Mine can show you true ones. But a true glimpse costs. Do you want to see further, or see clearer?"

choices.text: Further: every path, to the end

effects.log: "Greedy," {npc} says, approving. {He} guides your hand to the first thread of a path you never took.

choices.text: Clearer: the paths I am on

effects.log: "Wise," {npc} says, a little disappointed. {He} pulls your own thread taut so you can see its grain.

events.text: Weaving further, you find the end of a path you nearly took long ago: you are old there, and alone, and famous, and the loom shows it so clearly you can smell the incense at the funeral. {npc} watches your face. "Most people cut that thread," {he} says.

effects.log: You cut it. The loom shudders and goes on. Nothing in your life changes, and you feel lighter all the same.
You leave it. "It was a life too," you say. {npc} looks at you for a long moment, and weaves the next thread more gently.

events.text: Weaving clearer, you see your own thread up close: every glimpse you ever ran is a little knot in it, and the knots are where you were most afraid. {npc} runs a finger over them. "Fear is not a flaw in the cloth," {he} says. "It is where you held on."

effects.log: You untie it, slowly. Something you were afraid of for thirty years stops mattering by the end of the afternoon.
"For what?" {npc} asks. "For the next time I am afraid," you say. {He} ties it, laughing.

events.text: Three threads are woven, and the great loom is ready. {npc} hands you the shuttle. "One pass," {he} says. "Your loom and mine become one. Every glimpse after this is true: the real odds, plain as daylight, and more of them. Or you can give the shuttle back."

mem.note: made the pass on the great loom

effects.log: The shuttle flies. Behind your eyes the little loom becomes a great one, and every path has its numbers on it.

choices.text: Make it, and thank the Weaver first

effects.log: "Nobody thanks the Weaver," {npc} says, flustered, and then makes the pass with you, both hands on the shuttle.

events.text: In the Divine Realm the Loom of Heaven is not a thing but a place, and you stand inside the cloth with {npc}. The gods' threads run past you, thick as rivers, tangled. "Even they do not see where they go," {he} says. "Make the pass, and you will."

choices.text: Make the pass, and straighten one god's thread

effects.log: You smooth a knot in a god's thread as you pass. Somewhere a storm that was coming does not come.

choices.text: Make the pass, and touch nothing else

effects.log: You make the pass and leave the gods' threads alone. {npc} nods. "Wiser than they are," {he} murmurs.

events.text: Long after the pass, {npc} finds you sitting at the edge of the loom, watching the paths you did not take run on without you. "You saw them all," {he} says. "Do you regret any?" Each of them, you know now, was someone's life. Just not yours.

effects.log: "Good," {npc} says. "Then the last glimpse is yours, when you want it. Not before." {He} goes back to the shuttle.
"Only one?" {npc} says. "You are doing very well." {He} weaves that one into a ribbon and ties it on your wrist.

events.text: {npc} weaves beside you in silence for a season. At the end of it {he} holds up your thread, clear and strong, with all its knots. "Most people," {he} says, "come here to see a different life. You came to see your own. It is a good one."

effects.log: You agree, and mean it. {npc} hangs your thread where the light is best, and leaves it there.

mem.note: showed me the Weaver's own thread

effects.log: {npc} hesitates, then shows you. It is very long and has no knots at all. "I was never afraid," {he} says. "I envy you."

events.text: Above the clouds, no protagonist has ever come for you. Then the System says, very quietly: "Warning. One more." On the cloud bridge of the Jade Pavilion stands {npc}, born up here, never once below, with heaven's gold in {his} eyes. "They wrote me for you," {he} says. "I read it."

effects.log: "That you lose," {npc} says. "On the last page." You smile. The System prints the word: [PROTAGONIST]. It sounds pleased.
{npc} does not kneel. {He} only bends, like a reed. "Good," {he} says through {his} teeth. "I hoped you would."

events.text: {npc} stands on the cloud bridge with heaven's gold in {his} eyes and frowns at you. "I know you," {he} says. "Heaven's Script has your name in an old hand, from another life, in red. It says you took the pen once. It says you bowed." The System is silent, which it never is.

effects.log: "Not before I have beaten you," {npc} says. It is almost friendly. The System starts counting again.

choices.text: Say you do not remember bowing

effects.log: "Then I will remind you," {npc} says, and draws. Neither of you strikes. Not yet.

events.text: {npc} shows you where heroes come from: a hall in the Jade Pavilion where a golden book writes itself, one page a year, and every page is someone's destiny. Yours are in red. "I am the last hero it will write for you," {he} says. "How do you want this to end?"

choices.text: With you beaten, and the book with you

effects.log: "Then you will have to steal it," {npc} says. You already have a page in your sleeve. {He} pretends not to see.

choices.text: With the book written by someone else

effects.log: {npc} stares. "There is no one else." "There is you," you say, and hand {him} a page you took. {He} keeps it.

events.text: The script says {npc} must face a great trial alone: a demon of the upper sky, which heaven sends for heroes to slay. You could let the demon do your work for you. The System waits, and for once it gives no advice at all.

mem.note: fought the demon at my side

effects.log: You fight it together, back to back, and win, and afterwards {npc} will not look at you. "Why?" {he} asks. "Because you are mine to beat," you say.
{npc} comes back from the demon's sky alive, scarred, and twice as strong. The script, in your sleeve, writes a new line on its own.

events.text: Late at night {npc} comes to your door with the page you gave {him}, and a brush. "I tried to write my own ending," {he} says, "and nothing came. Heaven has always written for me." {He} looks younger than {he} is. "Teach me how a villain does it. You have been writing your own all your life."

effects.log: You teach {him} to want things heaven did not give {him}. It is the most villainous lesson you know. {He} writes a line, then another.
"Villains learn alone," you say. {npc} goes away and comes back a month later with a page in {his} own hand. It is not bad.

events.text: Every page you need is in your hands, and the golden book's last page is open on its stand: the ending, still blank, waiting for heaven. {npc} stands across the hall with a drawn sword. "Take the pen," {he} says, "or I will." The System says: [THE PEN: TAKE IT?]

effects.log: The pen is heavy and warm. Heaven's Script falls silent. {npc} lowers {his} sword, very slowly. "So that is what it looks like," {he} says.

choices.text: Take the pen, and leave the ending blank

effects.log: You take the pen and write nothing. {npc} lets out a breath {he} has held since birth. The last page stays empty, for both of you.

events.text: In the Divine Realm the golden book is the size of a sky, and the gods themselves come to read the last page of your story. {npc} stands beside you, not across from you, for the first time. "They want to see you lose," {he} says. "Shall we disappoint them?"

choices.text: Take the pen in front of the gods

effects.log: You take Heaven's pen in front of every god who came to watch. Not one of them says a word. {npc} laughs out loud.

choices.text: Take the pen, and hand it to {npc}

effects.log: You take it, and give it straight to {npc}. The gods murmur. "Now it is both our story," {he} says, and writes nothing.

events.text: With heaven's pen in your hand, nothing is written for {npc} any more, and {he} fights you anyway, every year, on the cloud bridge, because {he} wants to. You win, usually. "One day," {he} says, picking {him}self up. "One day I will write that I won."

effects.log: You let {him} win, once, and {npc} knows, and is furious, and the whole Jade Pavilion talks of nothing else for a decade.
"Then write better," you say. {npc} grins. The System pays you for every bout, and you hardly notice any more.

events.text: {npc} writes now. Not heaven's book, only a little notebook of {his} own, full of heroes heaven never wrote, and in every story there is a villain with your face who is not quite as bad as everyone thinks. "Do you mind?" {he} asks.

effects.log: "Good," {npc} says, and keeps writing. "A villain has to say that." You both know the stories will be told below for a thousand years.

choices.text: Ask to be the hero in one

mem.note: asked to be the hero in one story

effects.log: {npc} laughs until {he} has to sit down. Then {he} writes it: one story where you are the hero. It is the worst one in the book. You love it.

events.text: Above the clouds the iron ring, cold since the old master went on, is warm one morning. A voice, very faint: "...I can smell it. The tea." Across the pavilion {npc}, a Tea Steward of the Jade Pavilion, is pouring for immortals. The ring burns. "That powder," the voice whispers. "It came from up here."

effects.log: You watch {him} all afternoon. {He} pours well, and once, just once, glances at the ring on your hand.
"Is it really you?" you ask. "Of course it is," says the faint voice. "Stand up straight." You have missed that.

events.text: The iron ring warms above the clouds, and the faint voice inside it is puzzled. "I know this place," the old master says. "I have been here before. With you, I think. In another life." Across the pavilion {npc}, the Tea Steward, drops a cup, and does not pick it up.

choices.text: Tell the ring it has been settled before

effects.log: "Then let us settle it better," says the voice. {npc} has gone very pale.

choices.text: Go and pick up the cup

effects.log: You pick it up and hand it back to {npc}. {His} hands shake. "You," {he} says, and nothing else.

events.text: {npc} comes to you at last, alone, with a teapot. "Ninety years ago a mortal came up the white stairs on a pass and bought a powder from me," {he} says. "I asked no questions. I wanted a manual of a sword that cut rain. I have it still." The ring is very hot. "What does the ring want?"

effects.log: "Then you will have it," the old master says, "if they will hear a ghost." {npc} sets down the teapot and bows {his} head.

choices.text: The truth, and then we will see

effects.log: "The truth first," the old master says. "Then I decide." {npc} pours three cups: one for the ring.

events.text: The Heavenly Court does not hear ghosts, but it hears an immortal, and you speak for the ring. {npc} does not deny anything. The manual is brought out in a lacquered box: a sword that cut rain, ninety years in a tea steward's cupboard. A judge asks what you want done.

choices.text: Ask that the manual go home

effects.log: The manual is given back under the old master's name. "That is all I wanted," says the ring, and sounds surprised.
The court strips {npc} of the pavilion and every title. {He} does not look at you as {he} goes. The ring says nothing at all.

events.text: Over three cups of tea {npc} tells the whole of it: the mortal on the stair, the powder, the manual, and the ninety years of tea poured for immortals who never asked where {he} learned to hold a cup so well. "I am not sorry enough," {he} says. "I have tried to be."

choices.text: Ask the ring what it thinks

effects.log: The voice is quiet a long time. "Honest, at least," the old master says. "More than my sworn brother managed."
You drink the ring's cup. "Rude," says the voice, delighted. {npc} almost laughs.

events.text: It comes down to the manual on the table, the ring on your hand and {npc} across from you. The old master speaks clearly for the first time since going on:"Ninety years I carried this. I would like to put it down. You decide how, student. You have earned it."

choices.text: Return the manual, and the master's name with it

effects.log: You read the old master's name aloud into Heaven's register. The ring is warm, and stays warm, as if a fire has been lit for good.

choices.text: Make {npc} return it with {his} own hands

mem.note: gave the manual back with my own hands

effects.log: {npc} puts the manual in your hands, and bows to the ring. "I am sorry," {he} says, and this time it is enough.

events.text: In the Divine Realm the register of names is carved in the sky itself, and the old master's name was struck out of it ninety years ago, the day the manual changed hands. {npc} has come with you, the box under {his} arm. The ring whispers: "Put me back where I was, student."

choices.text: Carve the master's name back into the sky

effects.log: You carve it, letter by letter, in a sky that remembers. The ring is warm for good. {npc} watches with tears in {his} eyes.
{npc} carves the old master's name back with a shaking hand, beside {his} own. "Now we are both in it," {he} says.

events.text: With the business settled, the old master's voice comes and goes in the ring like weather. "I am still going on," the voice says one night,"only slower. I wanted to see what you would become." {npc} sends a cup of tea every year now, with no message.

effects.log: You drink it. It is very good tea. "Of course it is," says the ring. "{npc} was always a better steward than a thief."
You pour it over the ring, the way you would at a grave. "Sentimental," the voice says, pleased. "Do not do it again. It rusts."

events.text: {npc} has asked the old master, through you, to teach {him} the sword that cut rain. "The one who bought my death with a powder," the ring says, "wants my sword." It is quiet a long time. "Well. Somebody should have it. You decide, student."

mem.note: was taught the sword that cut rain

effects.log: You teach {him} the forms on the cloud terrace, and the ring corrects you both. It is the strangest school above the clouds.
"Good," the ring says. "Some things are not for sale twice." {npc} bows and does not ask again.

events.text: Above the clouds a sound reaches you through every wall: one hammer stroke, then silence, then one more, a full minute apart. At a forge on a floating rock {npc}, the Smith of the Hundred-Year Hammer, is making a nail. "A thousand years," {he} says, without looking up. "Same nail. Every time a little better."

effects.log: You watch for a day. The System opens a window you have never seen: [SMITHING: 0.0001%]. {npc} grins.

choices.text: Ask why anyone would do that

effects.log: "Why does anyone do anything twice?" {npc} asks. You do not have an answer. {He} goes back to the nail.

events.text: {npc}, the Smith of the Hundred-Year Hammer, stops in the middle of a stroke when you walk into the forge, for the first time in four hundred years. "I know your hands," {he} says. "They filled the last bar here once. In another life. Then they came back empty."

effects.log: "You will not need showing," {npc} says. "Hands remember." {He} hands you the hammer.

choices.text: Say you would rather learn it new

effects.log: "Good answer," {npc} says, and the hammer comes down again, exactly on time.

events.text: {npc} shows you what gold bars become up here, if you keep at them: jade, which no bar below the clouds has ever reached. "Gold is when you stop thinking," {he} says. "Jade is when you stop being someone who does the thing and become the thing. Which do you want first?"

choices.text: The bar I use the most

effects.log: "Practical," {npc} says. {He} makes you do it a hundred times, badly, then once, well.

choices.text: The bar I love the most

effects.log: "Sentimental," {npc} says, approving. {He} makes you do it once, slowly, the way you did it the first time.

events.text: Practice above the clouds is long and dull and {npc} allows no shortcuts. "The System sells gilded habits," {he} says. "Buy one and I will throw you off the rock." For a whole season you do the one thing, and the jade bar creeps.

effects.log: You keep going. One morning you notice you have stopped counting. {npc} notices too, and nods.

mem.note: took a day of rest with me

effects.log: "Rest is a bar too," {npc} says, and takes the day with you, which {he} has not done in a century.

events.text: You go back to the oldest thing you know how to do, the first habit of this life, and do it the way you did as a child, slowly, on purpose. {npc} watches, and for once does not correct you. "That one," {he} says, "you never needed a System for."

effects.log: You do it again. It is not better. It is yours. The jade bar fills a little anyway, as if it agreed.
{npc} is terrible at it. {He} has been doing one thing for a thousand years. {He} laughs like a child.

events.text: The bars you turned to jade hang in the air of the forge like green fire. {npc} puts down the hammer. "The System has one bar it never showed you," {he} says. "The one under all the others. [LIVING]. Jade bars feed it. Fill them all a little, and it fills too."

mem.note: struck the anvil once beside me

effects.log: You strike together, on time. Every bar you ever began leaps forward. In the window, [LIVING] moves for the first time.
You strike it alone, and it rings like a bell. The bars leap. {npc} closes {his} eyes and listens to the note.

events.text: In the Divine Realm {npc} brings the anvil up the last stair with you, because a smith does not leave the anvil. The gods have bars too, and most are empty: they have never practised anything. "Show them," {he} says. "One stroke."

choices.text: Strike, and let the gods see

effects.log: You strike once and every god in earshot feels it in their hands. The bars leap. [LIVING] moves. Some of the gods pick up tools.
You strike quietly. The note is for you and {npc}. The bars leap anyway. {npc} smiles.

events.text: Years on, your jade bars are steady, and {npc}'s nail is a little better than it was. "You did the useful ones," {he} says. "Now there is only the last one." The window shows [LIVING], further along than any bar you have ever had. It is not full. It does not have to be. Not yet.

effects.log: You go back to work. It is the most ordinary thing in the world, and you have never been better at it.
You sit and watch it a while. {npc} sits with you. Neither of you says anything for a year.

events.text: {npc} has started a second thing, after a thousand years of one: the habit you taught {him}. {He} is still terrible at it. "Four per cent," {he} says proudly, showing you a window only {he} can see. "In a thousand years I will be quite good." The bar called [LIVING] hums in your own window.

choices.text: Promise to come back and check

mem.note: promised to come back in a thousand years

effects.log: "In a thousand years," {npc} says. "Do not be late." The hammer comes down, exactly on time.

choices.text: Tell {him} four per cent is good

effects.log: {npc} goes red to the ears. "It is not," {he} says. "It is a start." You both know it is the same thing.

events.text: Above the clouds the years run so slowly that once, at dawn, they touch the years of the far house. The jade on your chest goes bright. A ripple opens in the clouds and {npc} steps out of it, in robes nobody has worn yet. "Ancestor," {he} says, and {his} voice is the voice you have heard in the jade for years.

effects.log: {npc} goes stiff, then holds on as if {he} was afraid you would fade. "You are warmer than I thought," {he} says.

choices.text: Bow, as to a head of the house

effects.log: {npc} bows back, lower. "You were never supposed to bow to me," {he} says. "The children will not believe it."

events.text: The jade blazes above the clouds and {npc} steps out of the light, and stops, and stares. "Ancestor. The house ledger says you met one of us before," {he} says. "In another life, above the clouds. It says you went home with them. And still the jade found you again."

choices.text: Say the house is worth finding twice

effects.log: {npc} laughs, a little wet. "That is what the ledger says you said last time too."

choices.text: Ask how the house is now

effects.log: "Better than it was," {npc} says. "Because of you. Twice." {He} takes your hands.

events.text: {npc} can stay only a little while each time the years touch. "I came to ask one thing," {he} says. "The house will be in danger again, in my time. The jade can carry letters both ways now, while you are up here. Will you answer them? Or would you rather I asked you something smaller?"

effects.log: "Then the first is already here," {npc} says, and gives you a folded page. You answer it before the ripple closes.
"Then tell me about the plum tree," {npc} says. "We never knew who planted it." You tell {him}. It was you.

events.text: The letters from the far house grow harder: a quarrel between branches, a sickness, an heir nobody wants. You answer them all as well as you can, and {npc} brings back what came of each. "The quarrel ended," {he} says once. "Because you said that thing about rice."

effects.log: You write a long letter to the whole house, not just the head of it. {npc} says they read it aloud at the new year.

mem.note: wrote a letter to the house with me

effects.log: {npc} hesitates, then tells you. It is better than what you would have written. You send it under both your names.

events.text: {npc} asks small things, every time: what you ate as a child, what you were afraid of, whether you sang. You answer, and {he} writes it all down for the house. "They think you were never afraid," {he} says. "I want them to know you were, and kept going."

choices.text: Tell {him} the truth about being afraid

effects.log: You tell {him} everything, even the parts you have never told anyone. {npc} writes it down very carefully.

choices.text: Sing {him} a song from your childhood

effects.log: You sing it, badly. {npc} learns it on the spot. Centuries from now, children will sing it wrong in the same places.

events.text: The last letter is answered, and the next time the years touch, {npc} does not come alone: behind {him} in the ripple you can see the far house, the courtyard, the plum tree, all of it safe. "It held," {he} says. "Because you answered. The jade wants to give you something back."

choices.text: Ask the jade to keep the house safe

effects.log: The jade blazes, and you feel the far house settle, centuries away, like a roof that will not leak again.

choices.text: Ask the jade to heal you again

effects.log: The jade warms against your chest the way it did when you were fifteen, and it does not cool again. {npc} looks relieved.

events.text: In the Divine Realm time is a river you can stand in, and {npc} comes up it on foot, with the whole far house behind {him}: dozens of faces, all of them yours a little. "Ancestor," {he} says, "they wanted to see you. Just once." The jade is brighter than the sun.

effects.log: You greet them all, one by one, and learn every name. It takes the whole day. Nobody in the house will ever forget it.
You kneel so the smallest ones can see you properly. One of them gives you a plum. {npc} has to look away.

events.text: The letters still come now and then, but they are only letters: news, gossip, a new child named after you, badly. {npc} visits when the years touch and stays as long as {he} can. "The house is yours to see," {he} says once. "If you ever want to come. You would not come back."

effects.log: "Not yet," you say. {npc} nods, as if {he} expected it. "The plum tree will wait," {he} says. "It is good at that."

choices.text: Ask {him} to stay a while longer

effects.log: {npc} stays until the ripple nearly closes on {him}, and jumps through at the last moment, laughing.

events.text: {npc} brings you a little book the house has made: every small thing you told {him}, the song, the fear, the rice, bound in green cloth. "The children learn it before they learn to read," {he} says. "They argue about which parts are true."

effects.log: "All of them?" {npc} asks. "Even the goose?" "Especially the goose," you say. {He} writes that in the margin.

mem.note: carried home a sealed page for the children

effects.log: You write one more page, for the children only. {npc} does not read it. {He} carries it home sealed.
